**Introduction**  
---

$name is a decentralised autonomous organisation (DAO) intended to implement Meritocracy in government organisations. The goal of $name is to and create an arena of competition between them which allows for promotion and consequent access to greater control of resources. The distributed ledger technology used in blockchain applications provides a pathway for achieving this, distributed ledgers can hold information – like examination scores – immutably and independently of central authority; this solves the problem of favouritism in Meritocracy. We can represent shares in the state, signifying ownership, with non-tradeable tokens so as to counteract Goodhart’s law, where metrics replace the thing they measure as goals. A variety of interactions between agents can be modelled by smart contracts which all take the basic form of a competition between two agents: a higher ranking agent may set an objective to be completed by multiple agents, or a lower ranking agent may challenge a higher ranking one to complete an objective relevant to their department. An optimistic oracle system exists according to a weighted voting system where those who hold more tokens have more votes . The goal of $name is to select leaders, it is not an actual means of conducting government and cannot replace human beings. 

---

**Meritocracy and Deep States**

---

Since the early 20th century, political theorists have identified the trend for effective power in industrial countries to move into the hands of unelected bureaucrats. This trend equally affected all countries, no matter their system of government, from the German monarchy to Liberal England. As these state employees serve for longer terms than elected representatives, they accumulate greater institutional knowledge and, thus, the ability to pursue policy independent of the nominal executive. In the early 21st century, public awareness grew about how these bureaucracies had become sympathetic to ideologies out of touch with the conditions of modern life and the customs of the majority. The term ‘deep state’, referring to these unelected state employees who influence policy to a far greater degree than any elected official, has migrated from Turkey to become a part of political discourse across the Western world. 

Furthermore, since the mid 20th century, Democratic systems have been forced to introduce an increasing number of anti-Democratic safeguards: like placing certain decisions in the hands of unelected judges, curbing freedom of expression when it is liable to cause disorder and banning political parties seen as threatening to Democracy writ large. When these safeguards become politicised, serving the ideological values of only one party in the democracy, the corrective aspect of the system is weakened. The opposition inevitably reaches the point where it becomes desirable to get rid of these safeguards, an effort usually requiring the seizure of extra-legal powers tantamount to a dictatorship.  

The difficulty in removing these officials and replacing them with political appointees is how to maintain impartial standards which ensures promotion happens by competence, instead of political patronage. The pre-professional forms of government in the West were, while less inept than older historiography maintained, short-termist and at least somewhat corrupt. If government posts become an open gift of patronage, a reformist government may have some initial successes but once the networks sustaining it break up there’d be a risk of long-term decay in institutional knowledge. 

While the United States has a tradition of (some) government posts being appointed, many European states have strong cultural norms of civil service impartiality, so that even if the law were changed to increase political control over the civil service, the political appointees would still be interacting with a layer of professionals who would replicate the deep-state problem in miniature. Even in the United States, large parts of the bureaucracy, like the State Department, remain professionalised. 

The solution offered by $name is to not only select officials by examination but to create a permanent record of ongoing examination, by competitive wagers to fulfil policy objectives set by the political layer, so that civil servants may compete for promotion as well as entry level jobs. In this way, the culture of institutionalised collective bargaining on which various ‘deep states’ are founded is undermined, with the cooperation of civil servants eager to advance above more politicised superiors. An objective record exists for the competence of any individual official which allows ministers to pick the best person for the job, without sacrificing standards of objectivity. $name, then, is an attempt to make the slogan of Meritocracy a reality 

A less ambitious version of this was attempted by the ‘New Management’ of the 1980s, which sought to use Public Choice Theory to examine the incentives guiding the behaviour of civil servants and, broadly, make public organisations function more like businesses. The problem with the New Management Theory is that it treated the budgets managed by civil servants as akin to the profits of a business, and the principle motive of civil servants being expanding their budgets and departmental headcount. In implementation, it focused on introducing quantitative benchmarks for the delivery of existing services, without always giving officials the power to actually change policy or changing how they were promoted. $name provides infrastructure in which various quantitative benchmarks can provide a direct feedback loop to policymaking.

**Distributed Ledgers as an Answer to the Problem of Succession**  
---

The distributed ledgers present in blockchain technology have, thus-far, been used predominantly in building alternative currencies and financial instruments; their application in government is still somewhat understudied. This is surprising, ‘bureaucracy’ means the ‘rule of offices’ and the history of bureaucracy is largely a history of record-keeping. Blockchains are, besides their dominant financial applications, principally a way of storing information. Information in a blockchain is stored on nodes across the system and verified by a consensus of all nodes. No one node can edit the state of the blockchain independently of these consensus mechanisms. Distributed ledgers are thus pertinent to solving the problem of Meritocracy as they provide a way for agents to rise through a hierarchy independent of their superiors, without undermining the rules of the hierarchy itself. 

The information we will be storing on the blockchain will be the ***rank*** of agents so as to decide problems of succession to sovereign authority. Rank will be measured by ***shares*** in the state which can be represented as ***tokens.*** As we are measuring our agents’ skill at ruling, they will be rewarded by their capacity to achieve objectives set by their superiors, or themselves, in competition with every other agent on the blockchain. These activities will form the transactions between agents (the methods used to model these transactions are covered in the chapter on ***smart contracts***). 

$name uses the ***Ethereum virtual machine*** via the Besu ethereum client. This allows the chain itself to be private according to a proof of authority protocol and run independently of Ethereum’s existing validators, thus preserving the independence and data integrity of transactions which will determine politically sensitive events. In this way, Ethereum validators have no influence over smart contracts on $name. Our current model for $name is of an individuated, personal-chain model similar to Nano in which each individual user has a separate chain and contracts are modelled as cross-chain events. 

$name is to Meritocracy what paper ballots are to Democracy, or double-entry accounting is to Capitalism. It is a way of measuring the performance of agents so as to ensure Meritocratic succession to offices. $name is not a market, it is a scoreboard. The purpose of $name is to select individuals for succession to posts with executive authority by peaceful competition. If agents had the ability to transfer shares to each other, they would no longer be a measurement of competence at governing but of competence at acquiring shares. As such tokens in $name are non-tradeable and uncapped.  This is a good place to detail the difference between Meritocracy and the broad swathe of Private-Law governance systems which have emerged since 2010\. In Meritocracy, sovereignty itself the agent of selection; setting objectives and, to an extent, choosing the ideal outcome. The successful players of a Meritocratic game have thus been selected according to how they perform for sovereignty, rather than the state itself being selected according to how it conforms to the mean idea of ‘good governance’ among a population.

**Token Generation**  
---

Even if we view ability as subjective, one would be forced to admit that if two people desire the same goal and one of them achieves it, that person has demonstrated an objectively better ability at the given trial (even if the conditions educating such abilities may’ve been outside of their control). One might say that the purest form of Meritocracy is Thrasymachus’s definition of Justice as the Right of the Stronger: with the only Meritocratic polities being those acquired by conquest. For all these reasons, we maintain that promotion in the Meritocracy must be attained by competition between agents, allowing agents freedom to innovate and improve upon how they answer directives. However, a ‘purist’ application of Natural Right can only lead to civil war, with each conqueror forfeiting his right to rule on death. For Meritocracy to work, free and peaceful competition for sovereignty must happen after an initial selection by examination.

The examination can expand to include any number of qualities we may find desirable in our future sovereigns. One can test for personality traits, like risk-taking or assertiveness and one could plausibly include the results of physical examinations as well as mental ones. It may be possible, in future versions of $name, to judge an applicant by physical attractiveness from an uploaded photo according to a weighted array of physical markers. 

However, for the initial version, the simplest means of selection must be a [RIOT I.Q test](https://www.riotiq.com). Not only I.Q is the strongest psychological measurement there is with the tightest correlation to other signifiers of competence; RIOT I.Q offers a free online tool to view and export test result data which we shall use to convert test data into tokens.

This ensures that it is not impossible for those with lower (still passing) scores to excel in the system by effort, while ensuring that competitive examinations play a just role in assigning responsibility within the system.

**Objectives and Orders**  
---

Objectives are off-chain events from which any contest is derivative. Objectives can be as vague, or precise, as the issuer wants: their resolution is independent of any algorithm. Wherever funds are being disclosed from a central account to the delegated budgets of Meritocrats, or keys to data commons, these must be tied to an Objective in $name. As such, all departments in a Meritocratic government would be tied to one or several Objectives. ‘Crime rate of 0.9%’ is an example of an Objective. Objectives live off-chain, on a central server and may, in a hybrid system, be posted by democratic politicians rather than posited by Meritocrats themselves. It is possible to imagine in ‘full Meritocracy’ that Objectives cost a certain amount of rank and may be set by Meritocrats themselves, creating dynamic policy formulation but for the purposes of this paper we shall assume they are set by a political layer living off chain. 

---

**Contests**   
---

***Contests*** are the means by which tokens are transferred from one Meritocrat to another. The basic type of contest in $name is a ***wager*** a three-way contract between a superior Meritocrat, who sets the wager, and two juniors. ***Wagers*** are tied to ***Objectives*** set by the political layer. When 2\< Meritocrats bid to complete an objective, they place a proportion of their tokens in escrow to be released to the potential winner. Each contestant then places a one-way prediction with a boolean YES/NO answer that they will win the contest. When the contest’s time period is over, whomsoever set the ***Objective*** determines which of the contestants won, triggering a smart contract which automatically releases the shares in escrow to the winner. Submissions and other standard policy documents can be attached as off-chain files to the Objective panel, via the GUI, detailing the proposals of the Meritocrats to achieving the objective which will be important in the dispute resolution mechanism. 

---

**Dispute Resolution**  
---

When the Chief Meritocrat decides upon who is the victor of a given contest, an eight hour dispute window is opened in which any Meritocrat – or any Meritocrat with an interest in the contest, may dispute the outcome by staking tokens proportional to those invested by all parties in the contest, the Chief Meritocrat may either accept the dispute, or initiate a vote in which 1 token \= 1 vote. In this way, Meritocracy is preserved throughout the process as those with higher exam results and more victorious contests behind them will have greater power to dispute outcomes.The weighted voting present in this dispute mechanism also ensures that the Chief Meritocrat must have enough tokens to successfully see off repetitive disputes to their rulings.

---

**Sub-Contests**  
---

A Meritocrat taking on a contest may split the tasks into sub-contests for lesser ranking Meritocrats. These succeed or fail independently of whether the Meritocrat succeeds on the main Objective. ---

**Competitive Governance**  
---

With this relatively simple architecture, a variety of tactics are open to Meritocrats. The assumed norm, under Meritocracy, is that any higher ranking individual may give orders to a lower ranking one as authorised by the Objective. If a lower ranking Meritocrat wishes to disobey these orders, they may submit an alternative proposal for meeting the Objective from which they were derived and enter into the contest. Higher ranking Meritocrats who wish to ‘take over’ the departments of rivals may enter into sub-contests under them, outperform them and thus steal their tokens.

	**The Political Situation in Britain**  
---

If built and deployed over the next five years, $name has the ability to influence the outcome of a Reformist government in Britain to a great degree. Reform U.K plan to transition the U.K civil service to a more American model by appointing Permanent Secretaries on four year contracts, giving ministers the power to sack civil servants, creating a Department of the Prime Minister and ending the doctrine of ministerial responsibility for the civil service. This plan will come under attack for a variety of reasons, some of which have been hinted at and Reform, at present, have no plan to deal with these attacks. 

There is a solid consensus that reforming the civil service is an essential precondition for fixing issues like immigration, free speech and national security in Britain. The challenge, as stated in **part I** is that the British civil service has had such a monopoly on government advice, containing both generalist policy advisors and administrative staff, that dispensing with the service altogether – while delivering on urgent issues for which the public expect swift remedies – is hard to imagine. Ministers may very well have the means to sack permanent secretaries but they are unlikely to have the staffing to sack Grade 4/5 officials (who ‘make the machine run’) and executive officers who perform administrative work. As such, the expertise of permanent officials in negotiating with the machine will remain valuable and political hires may find themselves underperforming for structural, rather than individual reasons. Previous efforts at reform have all become bogged down in procedure, as the argument is effectively made by the service that ‘reforming government’ is taking up resources which could go towards actually solving the problems at hand. The effective deployment of this argument saw the, slow and painful, demise of the Civil Service Department; the desiccation of Edward Heath’s business advice committee and the stalling of Lord Rayner’s early reforms under Margaret Thatcher. 

Current proposals which envisage a wholly political service entail making the civil service accountable to Parliament. This seems like an innocuous, perhaps even laudatory, development but could easily backfire. Without a clearly defined precedent (as with U.S congressional hearings) of how appointees may be scrutinised, parliamentary accountability could easily see non-parliamentary courts, or the unelected upper house, challenge the appointment of officials and distract the incumbent government with lawfare. Recent attempts, with widespread media cooperation, to stigmatise political donations received by Reform U.K point to the direction in which appointees in a political service will be attacked. There will be a strong argument, advanced by the press, that appointees will have gotten their jobs due to donations. 

$name offers a solution to each of the problems identified as facing a reformist government. Although ministers would have the power to choose which civil servants occupy which roles, they would do so through an anonymous and impartial ledger of competence. Furthermore, civil servants could directly improve their results on the ledger by competing on objectives. This means $name is incentivising existing civil servants themselves to support the project of reform. By allowing sympathetic civil servants to outcompete the resistants, it gives a fairly impartial justification for removing recalcitrant elements. $name does not, even, have to be compulsory for all members of the service although it would require aggressive promotion and moral support from the centre of government; provided ministers had the ability to appoint permanent secretaries (as current proposals say they will) $name will simply provide an un-tamperable ledger of anonymous potential candidate’s competence to fill these roles.
